title: UUID Generator: Generate V4 UUIDs Online Free
description: Free UUID generator to create random v4 UUIDs and GUIDs for databases, APIs and unique keys, in your browser. Private, instant, no uploads.

sections.heading: Every Row Deserves a Truly Unique Key
paragraphs: Databases, events and API resources need identifiers that never collide. Generating UUIDs provides 128-bit keys that are effectively unique everywhere, no coordination needed.
The v4 variant draws from cryptographically random bits.
ChooseTools generates UUIDs locally in your browser, in bulk.
Unlike sequential integers, UUIDs do not require a central authority to assign values, making them ideal for distributed systems that operate across regions and databases.

sections.heading: How to Generate UUIDs
paragraphs: Instant keys on demand.
Choose how many UUIDs you need and generate. Copy them as a list, comma-separated or line-separated, whichever your schema expects.
Generation is local, using your browser's randomness.
You can produce a single identifier for a quick test or generate thousands at once for seeding a staging database, all without leaving the page.

sections.heading: UUID v4 Format in One Glance
paragraphs: A v4 UUID reads like a 36-character string of hex and hyphens: 8-4-4-4-12, with a fixed version digit.
The recognizable structure makes them easy to spot in logs and databases.
Format validation happens automatically.
The version and variant bits are set according to RFC 4122, so any standards-compliant parser will accept the output without modification.
Uppercase and lowercase hex both pass validation, so the generator can emit whichever style your linter or style guide prefers.

sections.heading: Primary Keys, Events, and Correlations
paragraphs: Distributed systems prefer UUIDs over sequential IDs to avoid contention and leaks.
Event IDs and request tracking stay unambiguous across services.
Unique identifiers simplify merging and replication entirely.
When two microservices write records independently, UUIDs eliminate the merge conflicts that sequential counters create, keeping replication safe and idempotent.

sections.heading: Faster Than Remembering, Safer Than Keys
paragraphs: No brainstormed nicknames, no reused IDs, no guessable increments.
Random UUIDs also resist enumeration attacks on public resources.
Identity that takes care of itself.
Because the identifiers are effectively random, an attacker cannot predict the next value, which removes an entire class of information-disclosure vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: Bulk Generation and Export Formats
paragraphs: Some projects need a handful of IDs while others require thousands for test fixtures or data migrations.

The generator lets you choose the exact count, then returns results in the delimiter your code expects: newline-separated for shell scripts, comma-separated for CSV imports, or plain text for clipboard pasting.
Producing large batches locally avoids the latency and exposure of sending data to a remote API and waiting for the response.
Seeding a test database in one session, rather than scripting a generator, lets you inspect a sample of the identifiers before committing them.

sections.heading: Version 4 Versus Other UUID Versions
paragraphs: UUID versions 1 and 2 embed a MAC address and timestamp, which leaks node identity and time information.
Version 3 and 5 are namespace-based and deterministic, useful when you need reproducible IDs from the same input.
Version 4 trades determinism for privacy by relying entirely on random bits, making it the default choice when no deterministic relationship is required.

sections.heading: Using UUIDs Across Languages and Frameworks
paragraphs: JavaScript, Python, Go, Ruby and Java all ship with native or library-level UUID support, so generated identifiers drop into any codebase without conversion.
Most ORMs accept UUID columns directly, and database engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL index them efficiently with appropriate strategies.
The portability of the format means one generator serves projects across the entire stack.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
paragraphs: Storing UUIDs as strings rather than native binary types increases storage and slows indexing, so choosing the right column type matters.
Hyphenated and unhyphenated variants both appear in the wild, and tools should handle the format the consuming system expects.
Some legacy systems use UUID v1, which leaks the MAC address; switching to v4 eliminates that exposure without changing application logic.

sections.heading: Private Identifier Production
paragraphs: Identifiers generate on-device, never logged by a server.
No upload, no account, no watermark — across platforms.
Randomness without record keeping.
When identifiers protect unreleased product data or internal test accounts, local generation keeps them off third-party logs and analytics trails.

faqs.q: What format do generated UUIDs have?
faqs.a: Standard 8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal format with the v4 version marker, e.g. xxxxxxxx-xxxx-4xxx-yxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx.

faqs.q: Are UUID v4 values cryptographically random?
faqs.a: Yes. Version 4 relies on random bits from the platform's strong randomness source.
Yes. Everything runs locally in your browser with no uploads or accounts.

faqs.q: How many UUIDs can I generate at once?
faqs.a: You can generate any count you need, from a single identifier to thousands, with output formatted for your use case.

faqs.q: Can I use these UUIDs in a PostgreSQL or MySQL database?
faqs.a: Yes. Both databases support UUID column types and accept the standard hyphenated format directly.

faqs.q: Is there any risk of duplicate values?
faqs.a: The probability of two v4 UUIDs colliding is negligible because each draws from 122 random bits, making duplicates practical to never observe in ordinary usage.
